abstract: Metabolism and mitochondrial remodelling are increasingly recognised as key regulators of stem cell identity, governing the balance between self-renewal and differentiation. Here we compared mitochondrial and metabolic properties of stem and progenitor cells from the male germline using transmission electron microscopy, quantitative proteomics and extracellular flux analysis. While the stem cell-to-progenitor transition was accompanied by increased mitochondrial abundance and cristae density, our analyses unveiled a remarkable and unexpected capacity for spermatogonial stem cells (SSCs) to engage oxidative phosphorylation. When oxygen availability was unrestricted, SSCs displayed markedly greater maximal and spare respiratory capacity than progenitors, despite comparable glycolytic flux. SSCs were also enriched for glutathione-dependent antioxidant enzymes and maintained lower basal mitochondrial superoxide levels than progenitors. Collectively, these findings challenge the view that SSCs are predominantly glycolytic and instead identify metabolic plasticity, marked by latent oxidative capacity and enhanced redox control, as a hallmark of the stem cell state.
